facts.statement: Bistahieversor is a genus containing only one known species, B. sealeyi, which was described in 2010 from Late Cretaceous rocks in New Mexico.
facts.quote: The genus contains only a single known species, B. sealeyi, described in 2010, from the Late Cretaceous of New Mexico.

facts.statement: The first remains attributed to Bistahieversor were originally described in 1990 as a specimen of the genus Aublysodon.
facts.quote: The first remains now attributed to Bistahieversor, a partial skull and skeleton, were described in 1990 as a specimen of Aublysodon.

facts.statement: A complete skull and partial skeleton found in the Bisti/De-Na-Zin Wilderness Area of New Mexico in 1998 are colloquially known as the "Bisti Beast".
facts.quote: Another complete skull and partial skeleton were found in the Bisti/De-Na-Zin Wilderness Area of New Mexico in 1998, known colloquially as the "Bisti Beast".

facts.statement: The genus name Bistahieversor is derived from the Navajo word for the Bisti/De-Na-Zin Wilderness Area, meaning "place of the adobe formations".
facts.quote: They named it Bistahieversor sealeyi. The name Bistahieversor comes from the Navajo , or "place of the adobe formations" in reference to the Bisti/De-Na-Zin Wilderness Area where it was found.

facts.statement: The specific epithet 'eversor' in the name Bistahieversor means "destroyer" in Latin.
facts.quote: Eversor, the latter part of the name, means "destroyer" in Latin.

facts.statement: Adult Bistahieversor are estimated to have reached a length of about 9 meters and weighed at least one ton.
facts.quote: Adult Bistahieversor are estimated to have been around 9 m long and weigh at least a ton.

facts.statement: A 2016 study by Molina-Pérez and Larramendi estimated the length of Bistahieversor at 9 meters and its weight at 3.3 metric tons.
facts.quote: In 2016, Molina-Pérez and Larramendi gave a length of 9 meters (29.5 ft) and a weight of 3.3 metric tons (3.6 short tons).

facts.statement: The extra opening above the eye in Bistahieversor is thought to have housed an air sac that would have reduced the skull's weight.
facts.quote: The opening above the eye is thought to have accommodated an air sac that would have lightened the skull's weight.

facts.statement: Bistahieversor possessed a complex joint at its forehead designed to stabilize the skull and prevent movement at that joint.
facts.quote: Bistahieversor also had a complex joint at its "forehead" that would have stabilized the skull to prevent movement at the joint.

facts.statement: Large olfactory bulbs in Bistahieversor indicate a heightened sense of smell, while elongated semi-circular canals suggest increased agility and sophisticated gaze stabilization.
facts.quote: Its large olfactory bulbs indicate a very heightened sense of smell, while the elongated semi-circular canals implied increased agility and sophisticated gaze stabilization while the head was moving.

facts.statement: Although Bistahieversor had small optic lobes, this feature is not considered a strong indicator of poor vision in the dinosaur.
facts.quote: The study noted that, while Bistahieversor had small optic lobes, this was not a strong indicator of whether or not this dinosaur possessed poor vision.

facts.statement: Bistahieversor is often classified within the subfamily Tyrannosaurinae as a derived tyrannosaur.
facts.quote: Bistahieversor is a genus of derived tyrannosaur often classified in the subfamily Tyrannosaurinae.

facts.statement: A 2024 reanalysis by Rivera-Sylva & Longrich, based on new data, placed Bistahieversor within the tyrannosaurine clade Teratophoneini alongside Labocania, Dynamoterror, and Teratophoneus.
facts.quote: In 2024, Rivera-Sylva & Longrich described new remains likely belonging to a novel species of Labocania. Their new data allowed for the reanalysis of Bistahieversor as a member of the tyrannosaurine clade Teratophoneini, in addition to Labocania, Dynamoterror, Teratophoneus, and two unnamed specimens from the Aguja and Two Medicine formations.

facts.statement: A 2025 study by Zanno and Napoli recovered Bistahieversor as a basal representative of the Albertosaurinae subfamily alongside Jinbeisaurus.
facts.quote: In their 2025 paper regarding the validity of Nanotyrannus, Zanno and Napoli consistently recovered Bistahieversor as a basal representative of Albertosaurinae alongside Jinbeisaurus.

facts.statement: Bistahieversor lived during the Late Cretaceous, approximately 75 million years ago in the Campanian stage, in what is now North America.
facts.quote: que vivió a finales del período Cretácico, hace aproximadamente 75 millones de años, durante el Campaniense, en lo que es hoy Norteamérica.

facts.statement: Bistahieversor is known from adult and juvenile fossils in the Kirtland Formation, with fully developed adults estimated to measure about 9 meters in length and weigh more than a ton.
facts.quote: Bistahieversor se conoce por resto fósiles de ejemplares adultos y juveniles de la formación Kirtland, completamente desarrollado debió medir unos 9 metros de longitud y pesar más una tonelada.

facts.statement: Geographical barriers such as the formation of the Rocky Mountains may have isolated southern Bistahieversor populations from more advanced northern tyrannosaurs.
facts.quote: Las barreras geográficas tales como la formación de las Montañas Rocosas puede haber aislado más al sur a Bistahieversor de los tiranosaurios más avanzados del norte.
